target_customer: Commercial drone makers and enterprises (mining, construction, agriculture, insurance) that wanted drone autopilot hardware, software and cloud analytics
problem: Military autopilots were expensive and closed, and hobbyist autopilots were not reliable enough for commercial use. Airware sold a customizable autopilot platform and later full enterprise drone workflows.
business_model: Hardware plus software licensing at first (autopilot priced at 4,000 to 7,000 dollars), later enterprise drone solutions with cloud services
product_category: Commercial drone operating system and enterprise drone software

founders.name: Jonathan Downey
founders.background_notes: MIT Technology Review (June 2013) calls him a former Boeing engineer who worked on the A160 Hummingbird unmanned helicopter and a commercial pilot.

founders.name: Brad Schiller
founders.background_notes: Listed as co-founder on the YC page. No background found.

exit.reason: The company said it ran out of financial runway while pivoting. TechCrunch reported its own hardware push was overtaken by DJI and senseFly eBee and it had laid off staff over two years.

competitors.name: 3D Robotics
competitors.what: Open source ArduPilot based drones and autopilots, ready to fly systems from 599 dollars
competitors.traction_then: Led by Wired's former editor Chris Anderson

competitors.name: DroneDeploy
competitors.what: Software to manage and coordinate fleets of drones

competitors.name: Lockheed Martin
competitors.what: Said to be working on similar autopilot style projects, with slow results

technical_complexity.rationale: A reliable Linux based autopilot with sensors and safety requirements for commercial use is hard for a small team, and the later hardware and cloud analytics stack added more.

defensibility.rationale: Early integrations and certified reliability helped, but open source autopilots like Pixhawk and ArduPilot and bundled manufacturer software eroded the edge.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: DJI and other manufacturers shipped bundled software that became good enough, per TechCrunch, and Airware's own hardware could not compete.

market_need_then: Commercial drone use was expected to open as FAA rules developed, and drone makers wanted a reliable customizable autopilot. Customers in 2013 included a French drone maker, a rhino tracking nonprofit and a Gates Foundation vaccine delivery project.

branding.domain_note: Exact airware.com. The domain did not resolve when fetched.

identity.voice_and_tone: Enterprise and technical; the founder compared the platform to DOS

branding.brand_signature: Positioned as the operating system for commercial drones

rebrands.why: Wikipedia says the company was incorporated as Unmanned Innovation; the date and reason are not given.

brand_strength.rationale: It was a recognized name in commercial drones with heavy trade press coverage, but no evidence of community or merch.

pivots.from: Autopilot and drone operating system for drone makers
pivots.to: Full enterprise drone solutions including its own hardware and analytics
pivots.why: TechCrunch says the company pursued its own hardware and analytics; competitors later made them obsolete. Pivot date not given.

outcome_analysis: Airware raised about 118 million dollars from Andreessen Horowitz, Kleiner Perkins, GV and later strategic investors such as Caterpillar and Mitsubishi, but its pivot from autopilot software to its own drones put it up against DJI and others. Layoffs ran for about two years and the company shut down on September 14, 2018, days after a Mitsubishi backed Tokyo expansion, saying it ran out of runway. A rescue sale or raise was reported as not found.
notes: Series A amount conflicts: MIT Technology Review and Wikipedia say 10.7 million, other reports say 12.2 million. Total raised is reported as 118 million by TechCrunch and Global Venturing, 101 million over 17 rounds by CB Insights and over 70 million after the Series C by eWeek, so rounds recorded here are incomplete (known gap includes a 2013 seed, Intel in 2015, Caterpillar in 2017, Mitsubishi in 2018). The post shutdown asset sale to Delair appears on Wikipedia only and is unverified, so exit.acquirer is null. Failure factor ran_out_of_money is stated by the company; others are from TechCrunch's reporting. The company site airware.com did not resolve when fetched, so its state is unverified.
